THE CENTRAL QUESTION

What remains after a mission ends?

A rover or lander may become silent, but its photographs, measurements, engineering tests and lessons can remain useful for decades. This project turns that idea into an interactive archive. The opening signal is fictional; the spacecraft, mission events and photographs are based on NASA records.

01 // MISSION BRIEFING

A signal from the past.

Mission Control has received a fictional archive signal from two worlds. Your task is to investigate three real robotic explorers whose missions have ended but whose hardware and discoveries remain part of space history.

PRIMARY OBJECTIVE

Recover three mission archives

Visit each location, study its photograph, read the mission record and scan the archive. Each recovered record adds a badge to your collection.

FIELD PRINCIPLE

Separate evidence from storytelling

The archive signal and the player's role are fictional. The mission dates, spacecraft, science results and NASA images are real. Use the source links to check the evidence.

Why were these machines sent?

01 — Test a landing

Surveyor 3 helped scientists understand the lunar surface before astronauts landed there.

02 — Test a rover

Sojourner demonstrated that a small wheeled robot could move across another planet and investigate nearby rocks.

03 — Search for ancient water

Opportunity examined Martian rocks and soils for clues about environments that may once have contained liquid water.

Important distinction: “Left behind” does not mean the missions were forgotten. These spacecraft were designed for remote exploration. When their operations ended, the hardware remained on the Moon or Mars, while their data continued to be studied on Earth.

03 // MOON ARCHIVE · ARTIFACT 01
SURVEYOR 3 / LUNAR LANDER

The machine that tested the Moon.

Before humans could work safely on the lunar surface, engineers needed evidence. Surveyor 3 arrived on the Moon in 1967 and used a camera and a mechanical sampler to investigate the ground.

QUICK DATA
6,300+TV pictures sent
18 cmMaximum digging depth
1967Landing year
1969Apollo 12 visit

Archive scan: mission record

MISSIONSurveyor 3 was an uncrewed NASA lunar lander. It launched on April 17, 1967 and made a soft landing on April 20, 1967.
LOCATIONIt landed in the southeastern region of Oceanus Procellarum, also known as the Ocean of Storms.
INSTRUMENTSIts main scientific tools included a television camera and a surface sampler. The sampler could reach about 1.5 metres from the lander and dig up to about 18 centimetres deep.
EXPERIMENTSUnder commands from Earth, the sampler dug four trenches and performed bearing and impact tests. These experiments helped scientists estimate how the lunar soil would support a spacecraft.
RESULTSurveyor 3 sent more than 6,300 television pictures. The tests suggested the surface was firm enough to support an Apollo Lunar Module.
LAST CONTACTNASA last received contact from Surveyor 3 on May 4, 1967, two days after lunar night began.
LEGACYApollo 12 astronauts landed nearby in November 1969. On November 19, they visited Surveyor 3 and brought selected parts, including the camera system and soil scoop, back to Earth for study.
Unexpected landing: During descent, Surveyor 3 bounced twice before settling on the surface. Its landing was still successful, and it went on to send thousands of pictures and conduct important soil tests.

Mission timeline

17 APR 1967

Surveyor 3 launches from Florida.

20 APR 1967

The spacecraft lands on the Moon and begins sending images.

04 MAY 1967

Last contact is received after lunar night begins.

19 NOV 1969

Apollo 12 astronauts visit the lander and retrieve selected components.

Why does this archive matter?

Surveyor 3 connected robotic exploration with human exploration. Its measurements gave engineers and scientists direct information about the lunar surface. The spacecraft became inactive, but the returned hardware could be examined in laboratories on Earth, extending the mission's scientific value.

04 // MARS ARCHIVE · ARTIFACT 02
MARS PATHFINDER / SOJOURNER

A small rover. A giant first step.

In 1997, Mars Pathfinder delivered Sojourner to the Red Planet. The mission showed that a wheeled robot could leave its lander, travel across another world and investigate rocks at close range.

83Martian days of operation
7Days originally planned
1997Landing year

Archive scan: mission record

MISSIONMars Pathfinder was a NASA lander mission designed to demonstrate a relatively low-cost way to deliver science instruments to Mars. It carried the Sojourner rover.
LAUNCHPathfinder launched on December 4, 1996. It reached Mars and landed on July 4, 1997, in the Ares Vallis region.
LANDINGThe mission used an airbag system to cushion the lander's impact. After landing, the spacecraft opened its petal-like panels and deployed ramps for the rover.
PURPOSESojourner tested mobile robotic exploration. It moved around the landing site to photograph rocks and soil and to take measurements.
INSTRUMENTIts Alpha Proton X-ray Spectrometer (APXS) helped study the chemical composition of rocks and soil. The mission also collected images and atmospheric and meteorological measurements.
RESULTSojourner operated for 83 days, far beyond its planned seven-day mission. It demonstrated that a small rover could work on Mars.
FINAL SIGNALThe final data transmission from Pathfinder was received on September 27, 1997. The mission was formally terminated on March 10, 1998, after attempts to restore communication.
LEGACYPathfinder and Sojourner helped establish techniques and confidence for later Mars rover missions.
Why use airbags? Mars is far away, and a lander cannot rely on a pilot to steer it onto a runway. Pathfinder's airbag system was designed to absorb impact and help protect the spacecraft during landing.

Mission timeline

04 DEC 1996

Mars Pathfinder launches from Earth.

04 JUL 1997

Pathfinder lands on Mars and begins surface operations.

83 SOLS

Sojourner operates for 83 Martian days, rather than the planned seven.

27 SEP 1997

The final data transmission from Pathfinder is received.

10 MAR 1998

The Pathfinder mission is formally terminated.

Why does this archive matter?

Sojourner was small, but its achievement was enormous. It proved that a rover could travel beyond its landing platform and examine several nearby targets. That demonstration helped make later, larger Mars rovers possible.

Review the mission record, then scan to add it to your collection.

05 // MARS ARCHIVE · ARTIFACT 03
MARS EXPLORATION ROVER / OPPORTUNITY

The rover that kept going.

Opportunity was designed for a short mission, but it explored Mars for almost 15 years. Its long journey revealed evidence that parts of ancient Mars had once been wet for extended periods.

90Martian days planned
15 yrsAlmost 15 years operating
45.16 kmTotal distance travelled

Archive scan: mission record

MISSIONOpportunity was one of NASA's Mars Exploration Rovers. It launched on July 7, 2003 and landed on Mars on January 24, 2004.
DESIGNIt was a solar-powered rover equipped with cameras and scientific instruments to examine rocks, soil and the Martian environment.
PLANNED LIFEThe mission was designed to last 90 Martian days and travel about 1 kilometre. It continued operating for almost 15 years.
DISCOVERYOpportunity found geological evidence that some ancient Martian environments had liquid water for extended periods. This helped scientists assess whether Mars once had conditions that could have supported microbial life.
JOURNEYBy the end of the mission, Opportunity had travelled 28.06 miles (45.16 kilometres), far beyond its original travel plan.
LAST SIGNALThe final communication was received on June 10, 2018, during a severe planet-wide dust storm that reduced sunlight reaching the rover's solar panels.
MISSION ENDAfter more than a thousand commands to restore contact, NASA declared the mission complete on February 13, 2019.
FINAL PANORAMAOpportunity's final panorama was made from 354 images taken between May 13 and June 10, 2018. It recorded the rover's surroundings shortly before communication ended.
Science caution: Finding evidence of ancient water does not mean scientists found life on Mars. It means some past environments may have had conditions that could have been suitable for microbial life.

Mission timeline

07 JUL 2003

Opportunity launches from Earth.

24 JAN 2004

Opportunity lands on Mars.

2004–2018

The rover studies rocks, soil and landscapes, travelling more than 45 kilometres.

10 JUN 2018

Last communication is received during a planet-wide dust storm.

13 FEB 2019

NASA officially ends the mission.

Why does this archive matter?

Opportunity showed how much a robotic explorer can accomplish when its systems continue working beyond the original plan. Its observations changed scientists' understanding of ancient Martian environments and left a detailed record for future researchers.

Review the mission record, then scan to add it to your collection.

THE BIG IDEA

A machine can stop moving, but its discoveries keep travelling through time.

These missions remind us that exploration is not measured only by how long a spacecraft operates. Their engineering tests, images and scientific records continue to help people understand other worlds.

PROJECT IMPACT

ECHOES OF THE UNKNOWN transforms space history into an interactive learning journey. It connects each piece of hardware to its mission purpose, scientific contribution, mission status and lasting legacy. The project also encourages players to compare evidence and understand why historical data remains valuable after a mission ends.

PROJECT FILE

What is this project?

ECHOES OF THE UNKNOWN is an interactive educational game about NASA robotic explorers and the scientific value of hardware and data that remain on the Moon and Mars.

Learning goals

  • Understand why historic spacecraft were sent to the Moon and Mars.
  • Identify the purpose of a lander, rover, camera and surface sampler.
  • Learn how scientists use images and measurements to study other worlds.
  • Compare planned mission lifetimes with actual mission performance.
  • Understand the difference between evidence of ancient water and proof of life.
  • Recognise that mission data can remain useful after a spacecraft becomes inactive.

How to play

  1. Read the mission briefing.
  2. Choose a destination on the mission map.
  3. Study the NASA photographs and mission record.
  4. Scan each archive to collect its badge.
  5. Compare the three explorers on the archive board.
  6. Complete a final challenge: pick a difficulty and beat the clock.
  7. Read your score and revisit the source records.

What makes this more than a quiz?

Players move through a story, examine real mission photographs, read longer scientific records, collect archives, compare the explorers and then test their understanding. The game combines space history, science communication, visual learning and basic interactive design.
